title: Common REPC Errors to Avoid
summary: Training on common errors agents make with the Real Estate Purchase Contract (REPC) in Utah. Covers earnest money issues, wire transfers vs cashier's checks, included items disputes, math errors, settlement vs closing confusion, HOA fees, compensation structure pitfalls, seller disclosures, PID disclosure requirements, appraisal issues, and buyer cancellation rights.

broker_guidance.scenario: Buyer wants to use wire transfer for earnest money
broker_guidance.guidance: Wire transfers have fees ($15-20 typically). The earnest money is not considered received until the brokerage has the receipt on their end. If sent on the due date, it may not show until the next business day. Plan ahead, especially around weekends and holidays. If settlement will be affected, put an addendum in initially to extend deadlines.
broker_guidance.client_language: Wire transfers work great for earnest money, but there are a couple things to know. There's usually a small fee, and it can take a business day to show up on our end. Let's plan ahead so we don't cut it close.

broker_guidance.scenario: Buyer wants to split earnest money across multiple contracts
broker_guidance.guidance: Each contract is a separate commitment. You cannot use one $5,000 deposit to cover five separate $5,000 earnest money commitments unless there is a written addendum stating that the $5,000 covers all five contracts. Otherwise it violates the contract and sellers could sue for their individual earnest money amounts.
broker_guidance.client_language: Each contract needs its own earnest money deposit. We can't split one deposit across multiple offers unless we get a specific written agreement from all sellers.

broker_guidance.scenario: Dispute over included items (curtains, rods, hardware)
broker_guidance.guidance: The REPC states all window coverings, curtains, drapery rods, window blinds, shutters, screen doors, storm doors, and awnings are included if mounted. Do not redundantly list these in 'Other Included Items' - it's already covered. If an item is mounted to the wall, it's assumed included unless specifically excluded. The house must be delivered in the condition it was in when under contract.
broker_guidance.client_language: The contract covers anything that's mounted to the walls or fixtures. If the seller wants to take something that's attached, we need to specifically exclude it in writing.

broker_guidance.scenario: Seller takes mounted items (mantle, fixtures) before closing
broker_guidance.guidance: If an item was mounted when the buyer viewed the property and wrote the offer, it must remain. The seller cannot remove mounted items unless specifically excluded in the contract. This includes mantles, light fixtures, and hardware. The contract requires delivery in the same condition as when under contract.
broker_guidance.client_language: Anything that was attached to the property when you made your offer needs to stay. If something's missing at walkthrough, we'll address it before closing.

broker_guidance.scenario: Water rights vs water shares on a property
broker_guidance.guidance: Water rights (well on property) are different from water shares (irrigation/personal property). Water shares can be retained by the seller - they are personal property and can be excluded. Title typically handles water share transfers. For VA loans with shared wells, the lender may require annual Board of Health certification that water is safe for consumption.
broker_guidance.client_language: Water rights stay with the property, but water shares are separate and can be kept by the seller. We'll make sure title handles any transfers properly.

broker_guidance.guidance: Double-check all math, especially with seller financing. Put zeros in blank fields (additional earnest money, seller financing sections) so it's visually obvious those sections aren't being used. This prevents confusion during review.
broker_guidance.client_language: I'll double-check all the numbers in the contract to make sure everything adds up correctly.

broker_guidance.guidance: Settlement is when everything is signed and money is delivered. Closing is when it's recorded by the county. There can be a gap - up to 4 days under contract. Buyers may assume they get keys immediately after signing. Avoid Friday signings when possible because if issues arise, it may not record until Monday. County recorder hours vary - some rural counties (like Juab) have limited hours.
broker_guidance.client_language: Signing day and getting your keys can be different days. The county needs to record the deed, which can take a few business days. We'll plan the timeline so you know exactly when you'll get possession.

broker_guidance.guidance: Two different HOA fees: 1) Reinvestment fee (goes into operating account, dollar amount or percentage of purchase price), 2) HOA transfer fee (for paperwork to set up new account). Utah now limits reinvestment fees for HOAs established in the last 3 years, but older HOAs may charge up to 1.5% of purchase price. Check the listing for accuracy - multiple listings in same development sometimes show different fees. The state now has an HOA Ombudsman through the Division of Real Estate for disputes.
broker_guidance.client_language: There are typically two HOA fees at closing - a transfer fee for the paperwork and a reinvestment fee that goes into the community's operating budget. I'll verify the exact amounts before we get too far along.

broker_guidance.guidance: Be very clear about compensation structure. If using percentage, put 'does not apply' in the dollar box. If using dollar amount, put 'does not apply' in the percentage box. Do not leave zeros in the unused field. An attorney successfully argued that 'percentage OR zero dollars' meant the buyer could opt for zero. This applies to REPC, Buyer Broker Agency Agreement, and ERS. VA buyers can now pay buyer agent compensation outside of closing (changed after Sitzer/Burnett cases).
broker_guidance.client_language: I'll make sure the compensation structure is crystal clear in all our paperwork so there's no confusion about who pays what.

broker_guidance.guidance: Agents must verify whether property is in a PID (Public Improvement District). This is a separate taxing district that can add significant costs over 20 years (example: $45-50K in additional property tax). New construction must disclose this. If not disclosed, buyers can back out. The developer creates PIDs to pay for roads, gutters, sewer improvements. All subsequent owners must also disclose the PID when selling.
broker_guidance.client_language: I'll verify whether this property is in any special tax districts. Some new developments have additional taxes that can add up to thousands over the years, and that needs to be disclosed upfront.

broker_guidance.guidance: If appraisal comes in below contract price, options include: renegotiating price based on appraisal, requesting reappraisal (especially if errors exist), or buyer making up difference. Document appraisal errors carefully - one case had no credit for solar panels, wrong square footage, and came in $35K below contract. The AMC eventually dropped that appraiser due to repeated errors. Lender supervisors can approve new appraisals on conventional loans.
broker_guidance.client_language: If the appraisal comes in low, we have options. We can renegotiate, challenge errors in the appraisal, or look at other solutions. I'll review the appraisal carefully to make sure it's accurate.

broker_guidance.scenario: Buyer cancellation after due diligence but before financing/appraisal deadline
broker_guidance.guidance: Buyers can cancel during the financing/appraisal period for any reason technically related to financing/appraisal, but there's no proof required. They don't have to prove they didn't qualify or that appraisal came in low. However, agents should not advertise this as a 'second due diligence period' - this has led to ethics cases and litigation. The contract says 'Buyer fails to obtain the loan' meaning proceeds were not delivered.
broker_guidance.client_language: The contract gives you a window to cancel if financing doesn't work out. Let's make sure we use that appropriately and document everything properly.

broker_guidance.scenario: Buyer wants to move in before closing
broker_guidance.guidance: Do NOT let buyers move in or store possessions before closing without proper protections. One case: buyers stored items in garage over weekend, then started remodeling. Monday underwriting did final credit check, buyers had new credit dings from Home Depot/Lowe's purchases, no longer qualified, and couldn't close. They had already damaged the property. If early possession is absolutely necessary, use an indemnity agreement and supervise carefully.
broker_guidance.client_language: I strongly recommend waiting until after closing to move anything in. If there's an absolute emergency, we'll need a formal agreement and I'll supervise the entire process.

steps: Verify earnest money form and amount
Confirm wire transfer timing or cashier's check acceptability with lender
Review included items - check mounted fixtures, don't redundantly list standard inclusions
Double-check all math, especially seller financing sections
Put zeros in unused fields for visual clarity
Verify settlement vs closing dates and county recorder hours
Check HOA fees: reinvestment fee AND transfer fee
Confirm compensation structure is clear (percentage OR dollar, not both/zeros)
Verify PID status for new construction
Review appraisal carefully for errors if it comes in low
Do not allow early possession without indemnity agreement

objections.objection: The title company said we can use one deposit for multiple contracts
objections.response: Each contract is a separate legal commitment. Unless we have a written addendum signed by all parties stating that one deposit covers multiple contracts, we can't do it. The sellers could sue for their individual earnest money if there's a default.

objections.objection: The seller took the curtains/rods - they said those weren't included
objections.response: The REPC specifically includes all window coverings and mounting hardware. If it was mounted when we wrote the offer, it's included. The seller needs to return them or compensate for replacement.

objections.objection: Why can't I move my stuff in this weekend? The house is vacant
objections.response: I understand the temptation, but if something goes wrong with financing or the deal, it creates huge liability. I've seen buyers lose their loan qualification after making pre-closing purchases, and then they're stuck with damaged property and nowhere to live. Let's wait until we have clear title.
